title: Comparative Genomics Analyses of Bacterial tRNA Modification Protein Families Using Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COG) and KEGG Orthology (KO) Classification Systems
content: Accurate identification of bacterial tRNA modification enzymes is essential for understanding translation, physiology, and genome evolution, yet annotation remains complicated by paralogy, multifunctionality, functional divergence, and non-orthologous replacement. We compiled an experimentally supported catalog of bacterial tRNA modification proteins and linked them to 71 Clusters of Orthologous Groups (COG) and 74 KEGG Orthology (KO) families. Their distributions, conservation, and copy-number patterns were examined across 1,322 bacterial genomes represented in both annotation systems. Comparison of COG and KO assignments revealed strong agreement for one-to-one family relationships but substantial discordance for broad COG families that encompass functionally distinct paralogs. Genome-scale profiling identified a conserved core repertoire of tRNA modification systems that was supported by both phylogenetic conservation and retention in bacteria with highly reduced genomes. Phylogenetic distribution patterns highlighted known and candidate cases of non-orthologous replacement, including alternative solutions for m5U54 and xm5(s2)U34 biosynthesis, and identified Actinomycetota as a promising source of currently uncharacterized tRNA modification enzymes. Gene-duplication analyses revealed that most core tRNA modification pathways were maintained as single-copy genes or highly conserved single-copy modules, whereas only a limited number of families, displayed substantial expansion. Predicted tRNA modification repertoires increased with genome size, but the relationship was weak, lineage dependent, and better described by log-linear than linear models, indicating diminishing gains in modification capacity with increasing genome complexity. Finally, phylogenetically informed analyses identified a small number of associations between specific tRNA modification pathways and physiological traits. Together, these results provide an updated COG-KO reference framework for bacterial tRNA modification systems, clarify the strengths and limitations of commonly used orthology resources, and highlight evolutionary processes shaping the diversification of bacterial tRNA modification pathways.
